That this House condemns the government for the lack of an effective economic program for these difficult times.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: PUBLICATION OF REPORT ON URANIUM CARTEL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice and Attorney General. It concerns the information which has been sworn regarding the uranium cartel, an action flowing from the report of the director of the combines investigation branch and from independent legal advice which the government sought.
The minister will remember that on March 4 his colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, promised that the full report of the director of the combines investigation branch would be made public. In order that Parliament may have all of the information about the uranium cartel and may understand why certain corporations and individuals were named and certain others, including past or present ministers of this government, were not named, will the Minister of Justice and Attorney General agree now to publish immediately the full report of the combines director and the full context of the independent legal advice which the government sought?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: PUBLICATION OF REPORT ON URANIUM CARTEL
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs never made such a promise to the House.

subsubtopic: PUBLICATION OF REPORT ON URANIUM CARTEL
speechtext: On March 4.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: PUBLICATION OF REPORT ON URANIUM CARTEL
speechtext: I have, however, received a report from the combines director, who was advised by a Toronto lawyer named John Brown. I also asked the same firm of lawyers to advise me on this matter. I have asked Mr. Brown to act as prosecutor in the cases he recommended that I prosecute, whose recommendation I have accepted. All of Mr. Brown's recommendations are included in the action which has been launched before the court, which will now be disposed of by the court.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL PROSECUTOR

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL PROSECUTOR
speechtext: Madam Speaker, what the minister is saying is that some lawyer he has chosen in Toronto has a right to see this report and has a right to knowledge of the independent legal advice that was made available, but the minister is hiding that report and that legal advice from the House of Commons of Canada.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL PROSECUTOR
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL PROSECUTOR
speechtext: The minister will know that among the unindicted co-conspirators are former public servants. The minister will also know that the cartel involved a "gag" order in council and other direct policy decisions taken by the Government of Canada. Since the Attorney General and Minister of Justice was a member of the government which set up that cartel, and which was involved in taking other decisions leading to this legal action, will the minister act to avoid any appearance at all of a conflict of interest and have this legal action pursued by a special prosecutor or by attorneys general who have no association whatever with the actions that will be considered by the courts?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
subtopic: REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL PROSECUTOR
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to clarify the statement made by the hon. member. The lawyer to whom I have referred is the same one who was hired by Mr. Bertrand and who has worked for four years on the case. He is the lawyer who made the report to Mr. Bertrand.
After I received the report from Mr. Bertrand, I asked the same lawyer, who had worked on the commission for four years, to be the prosecutor. This lawyer who worked on the inquiry for four years is the same one I have hired to be the special prosecutor in this file. Both in the report made to Mr. Bertrand, which was transferred to me, and in the special report that was made to me after I hired the same lawyer, that lawyer recommended that I prosecute the same companies. I have accepted his recommendation. This prosecutor is the same person who conducted the inquiry. He has accepted the position of special prosecutor in this case, and I am very pleased that he has done so.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, now we know who they are. They are Mr. Brown and Mr. Bertrand. But we do not know what they said. This House of Commons has a right to know what was said in those reports, which involved information being laid against certain corporations and individuals but not information being laid, for example, against the Minister of Justice, against the former minister of energy, mines and resources and against the Prime Minister. He points to himself. He has perhaps read the report. The members of the House of Commons would like the opportunity to read the report.
July 8, 1981

My question stands as to whether the minister will now end the secrecy and publish the report. While he is considering that question which was asked some time ago, let me ask him a question which goes to the heart of our system of responsible government in this country. Two former public servants are named as unindicated co-conspirators for actions taken during the period that they were public servants. One was an ADM at the time. Obviously they had to be acting on the instructions of the cabinet to which they were responsible. Will the minister explain why, when former public servants are named, the Prime Minister and present and former ministers of the government to whom those public servants were responsible are not named?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: In my opinion, Madam Speaker, the answer is very easy. Mr. Brown and the other lawyers who worked with him on this case made recommendations to me and I followed all of them. I ordered that legal action be taken against the companies, as recommended by Messrs. Bertrand and Brown, and I accepted their recommendations exactly as they were. At no time did the commission or the director himself feel that there had been anomalies in the conduct of the ministers or of other persons, except those referred to in the lawsuit. I therefore accept Messrs. Bertrand's and Brown's report, and I have launched proceedings in line with their recommendations. I cannot do any better than to follow the advice of people who have spent the last four years scrutinizing thousands of documents and pages of evidence they received. They have recommended that the six companies be prosecuted and that is exactly what I have done.

subtopic: KNOWLEDGE OF SENIOR OFFICIALS AND MINISTERS
KNOWLEDGE OF SENIOR OFFICIALS AND MINISTERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is also to the Minister of Justice and, most important, the Attorney General of Canada. The essence of the information of the charge that has been laid is the fact that it has apparently come to the attention of the combines investigation people that the accused had knowledge that the cartel activities affected the Canadian market. In particular, Mr. Mac-Nabb, a co-conspirator, and Mr. Runnalls, a co-conspirator, according to the information, had knowledge that the cartel affected the Canadian market. Will the Attorney General indicate to the House how he determined that nobody senior to Mr. Runnalls or Mr. MacNabb had similar knowledge that the cartel had affected the Canadian market, including Mr. Austin, the deputy minister, Mr. Macdonald the minister, and the Prime Minister who, of course, presided over the whole cabinet deliberations when the conspiracy was put in place? Why were they not joined as co-conspirators?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
subtopic: KNOWLEDGE OF SENIOR OFFICIALS AND MINISTERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Mr. Bertrand and the
Oral Questions
outside lawyers worked on the files for four years. They examined thousands of documents and talked to a lot of witnesses. They concluded that the charges should be put in front of the court the way they have been. I am not about to have a trial in this House of Commons when we decide to prosecute companies or individuals. The matter is being decided before the courts. If the hon. member is very interested, when the case is being heard in Toronto he might sit there and learn a little more.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary is to the Attorney General of Canada, and I emphasize Attorney General of Canada, who should at least be neutral in this case. Will the Attorney General confirm to the House that, first, Mr. Bertrand was denied access to cabinet minutes and other cabinet documents that have shed some light on who was aware of the effect of the cartel in Canada and, second, whether he personally in his role as Attorney General reviewed those cabinet minutes to determine whether others within cabinet were implicated, as has been indicated today?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I must say that there are rules and customs with respect to minutes of the cabinet. Mr. Bertrand did contact the cabinet officials at the time and he himself declared that the minutes of the cabinet meetings were not essential to carry out his mandate. In the circumstances, they completed their inquiry. They also made recommendations to me and I accepted them as they were. The case is now before the courts and it will be up to them to decide whether or not the six companies involved broke the law of Canada.

subsubtopic: POSTAL STRIKE-OFFER TO HAVE NEW CROWN CORPORATION PRESIDENT ENTER NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the President of Treasury Board. Considering that this morning the postal workers took an important conciliatory step in terms of reaching, one hopes, a settlement that will stop the postal strike, the step being the proposal that the president-designate of the new Crown corporation to run the post office be included as part of the government's negotiating team, I would ask the minister whether the government will match this good will offer of the postal workers by agreeing to it?

July 8, 1981
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: POSTAL STRIKE-OFFER TO HAVE NEW CROWN CORPORATION PRESIDENT ENTER NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, indeed I am very pleased with the conciliatory step which has been taken by CUPW in suggesting that the pre-conditions will be removed before we return to the table. The additional condition which it has stipulated, the presence of Mr. Warren, causes us, I must say frankly, some reservations which I have been discussing with my colleagues. I can assure the House that I have responded to Mr. Parrot's letter in the most positive terms, thanking him for their efforts at conciliation and hoping to provide some other means of establishing the conditions which would not be as difficult for us to accept.

Madam Speaker, will the minister elaborate on the last part of his answer? Considering that Mr. Warren is a man with considerable industrial relations experience, would it not make perfectly good sense, given that background on the one hand, and considering that he is about to run the new post office on the other hand, for him to be involved precisely at this point in the negotiations, especially if this can get negotiations under way again in order to put an end to the postal strike?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is essential that the position of Mr. Warren, the long-term interests of the post office, and relationships between the union and the post office be on the best terms possible, and it is important that such position not in any way be prejudiced. Accordingly that is why my colleagues and I have been consulting on this request that has been made. I must say we find it somewhat unusual that CUPW would suggest that it should determine who the members of our negotiating team should be.

Madam Speaker, with regard to just the last part of the answer from the minister, that is the disturbing kind of note that hopefully everyone on both sides of this House, as well as the post office and postal workers, wants to avoid. If the postal workers have withdrawn an important pre-condition which they have laid down for the past week or so, then they have taken an important step forward. What I am at a loss to understand is why the minister is not prepared to match this good will gesture by saying, "Yes, given Mr. Warren's past negotiating experience, and given the importance of resolving this dispute to all the people of Canada who are affected by it, especially the postal workers, we will go ahead and do that"?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thought I had answered that question in the first instance. I do not think the hon. Leader of the NDP has considered all the implications of that particular request. I believe it is our responsibility as a government, not just as President of the Treasury Board, to hold consultations
with the Postmaster General and other colleagues who should be consulted on this matter, and I can assure the hon. member that I do accept with gratitude that there has been some movement on the part of the union. I have responded in writing to Mr. Parrot's request, but I do not think the floor of the House of Commons is the proper forum within which to carry on this kind of negotiation.

subsubtopic: URANIUM CARTEL-NAMING OF UNINDICTED CO-CONSPIRATORS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice, who is behind the curtains. I wonder if I could await his arrival.
The Minister of Justice is the only individual in this House who knows why Mr. Brown recommended that these six corporate accused be charged. In light of the fact that, according to the indictment, the conspiracy took place partially in Ottawa, and two senior officials of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Gordon MacNabb and John Runnalls, are named but as unindicted co-conspirators, I would like to ask the Minister of Justice why they have been named but not charged.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
subsubtopic: URANIUM CARTEL-NAMING OF UNINDICTED CO-CONSPIRATORS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, this is not unprecedented. It has happened on many occasions in the past that decisions like that have been made. It was the recommendation of the commission and of Mr. Brown, as he acted as a special prosecutor for me in that case, to proceed that way, and I have accepted this recommendation.

subsubtopic: URANIUM CARTEL-NAMING OF UNINDICTED CO-CONSPIRATORS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, what I want to know are the reasons Mr. Brown gave to the Minister of Justice for not charging these individuals and yet naming them in this indictment.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT ORDER IN COUNCIL BE RESCINDED
REQUEST THAT ORDER IN COUNCIL BE RESCINDED

speechtext: My question is directed to the Prime Minister. I wonder if he could tell us at what point in time did the government of which he was head become aware that the activities of the cartel were affecting not only the international price-which he quite rightly said is not illegal- but at what point in time did he become aware that those activities may have also been affecting the domestic price?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DATE WHEN GOVERNMENT BECAME AWARE OF CARTEL'S DOMESTIC EFFECT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I cannot say this out of knowledge or out of memory. I can say, out of subsequent information 1 received, that it was likely around 1975. It was several years, I think three years after the international agreement had been made, that this international cartel began to have some possible effects within our country. Once again, I am repeating information I received at the time, and which would have to be checked for accuracy of dates. Until then, there had been no demand for uranium in Canada. It was only around the mid seventies that this demand arose.
Once again I refer to the judgment cited by the Attorney General earlier in this Question Period. It was judged that the regulations that we had made regarding the international cartel did not apply to actions to fix prices in Canada. At some point, long after the government had created this international cartel, there was a possibility of fixing prices in Canada. He said: Madam Speaker, in moving that Bill S-10 receive third reading at this time, I should like to call attention to all the co-operative effort that has gone into getting the bill to this point in the legislative process. I have in mind the recent deliberations at second reading, slightly more than two weeks ago, when a number of hon. members from the other side rose to express their views on this bill to amend the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act or, as we call it, CALURA. The same spirit of participation continued to manifest itself as the bill received further review and study before the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
During the last two days of June the committee worked hard to further improve the legislation wherever possible.
[ Translation]
Thanks to those exhaustive deliberations the committee was able to complete its work rapidly and tabled its report last Thursday, July 2.
Mr. Speaker, according to the report, the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates had adopted two rather significant amendments. The first, under clause 3(1 )(a), raises the threshold of corporate returns from $5 million in assets, as was originally proposed, to $10 million, and from $10 million to $15 million in gross revenue. The second, under clause 3(1)(6), also raises the threshold of corporate returns on the basis of equity or long-term debt obligations of persons not resident in Canada from a total amount of $100,000 to a ceiling of $200,000 for various equities and long-term debt obligations owing to persons or associates not resident in Canada.

I have cited the substance of these two amendments so that the considerable benefits that flow from them will be fully appreciated. The overriding benefit is relief from paperwork for more than-would you believe-96,000 Canadian-owned corporations, 6,000 more than was the case before the committee began deliberations a few short days ago.
When this legislation was first introduced in the House some three and a half years ago-it has been a long time coming-as Bill C-7, it was estimated that some 70,000 relatively small Canadian-owned corporations would be exempted from reporting under CALURA.
The threshold for reporting now proposed-that of $10 million in assets or $15 million in sales-is more in line with the conditions prevailing today and the original intent of the act.
It is a source of satisfaction to me that, numerically, the greatest relief from reporting will take place in those industries
Corporations and Labour Unions
where the smaller, Canadian-owned company is most prevalent. Coming from northern Ontario where most corporations are small, I am pleased that the impact of this bill will be felt in rural regions, including the northern region of this province.
Based on estimates related to corporate activity in 1978, we find that 11,420 Canadian-controlled companies in the construction industry will be exempt; only 526 will be obliged to report, along with 205 foreign-controlled companies. Similar generous exemptions will prevail in the wholesale, retail and services industries. The most dramatic decrease in the reporting requirement will come within the agriculture, forestry and fishing segment. On the same basis, there will be exemptions for 5,113 Canadian corporations, leaving only 56 corporations to report.

Overall, 96,800 Canadian-owned companies will be exempt from reporting if Bill S-10 is passed in its present form.
And now, Mr. Speaker, given those significant figures, we have every right to ask the following question: Will there be enough companies left to report under CALURA so as to appropriately meet our needs? In other words, will CALURA have the same impact and the same raison d'etre after those exemptions? Let me assure the House that the integrity of CALURA will not be jeopardized in any way.

We have made an analysis based on the new threshold. It shows that in terms of assets, over 81 per cent of all corporate activity in Canada will be recorded on the CALURA questionnaire. Notwithstanding the 96 corporations that we have eliminated, I repeat, 81 per cent of corporate activity will be caught by the statute.
Pursuing the analysis industry by industry, we discover that future reporting under CALURA will include companies with over 85 per cent of all manufacturing assets, in mining, approximately 95 per cent and in utilities about the same percentage. In the entire non-financial segment, over 76 per cent, and in the finance sector 85 per cent, will be required to report. We, therefore, have a happy situation whereby through Bill S-10 we can exempt all but 17,000 Canadian-owned companies and at the same time capture the information considered essential.
To conclude this review of the new thresholds and their impact on business, I should like to point out that under the bill before us today there will be slightly more than 9,000 foreign-owned companies that will be liable to report ownership data-and I do stress, ownership data. Canadian-controlled corporations that also have to report would total just under an; under an amended CALURA and under the proposed amendments, less than 8,000 companies will have to report consolidated financial information. Only about 2,000 companies will have to complete the schedules on technology transfer.

In other words, with passage of Bill S-10 we will have a streamlined, up-to-date piece of legislation providing us with the information we need with the least possible amount of paperwork.
1 hope that we can conclude third reading of this bill today. These amendments, having been in the legislative process for years, are now ready. As I have indicated, their time has come. I reiterate what I said earlier, that I appreciate the co-operation and the contribution that has been made in improving this bill by members of the committee. The bill has come out of committee improved, although at the outset when proposals were being made I had some doubt. We now have an up-to-date bill which we have been trying to get through the legislative process for about three and a half years. Hopefully, we are now in the last 20 or 25 minutes of debate on it. 1 would be very pleased if it were possible for this bill to be passed this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few brief comments to make on third reading of Bill S-10. In many ways I support what the minister has said. In fact, I think we have before us today an example of what can happen in this place sometimes when there is some co-operation between the government of the day, the minister of the day and all members of the House of Commons. I do not think there has been any serious disagreement that some bill in the form of S-10 is overdue. The main disagreement was whether we were sure that the threshold limits as originally proposed in Bill S-10 are low enough to ensure that many of the comparatively small businesses will not be caught up in this unnecessary paper burden in the future.
As the minister indicated during the committee hearings, there was discussion and then agreement that there should be amendments raising the threshold in the case of revenue in each company from $10 million to $15 million a year and in the case of assets raising the limit from $5 million to $10 million per year. In the case foreign subsidiaries, there was a rather complicated section which would have required companies doing business here who happen to have a mere $200,000 of foreign investment to file in accordance with the act. We were able to get the minister's agreement and also the committee's agreement to have that requirement amended so there is a much more reasonable threshold limit all round.
In short, I see no reason to delay the bill further. I hope the Senate will agree with the changes that have been made in this House.
In handling this bill in future months and years, I hope the minister will always bear in mind, and he gave us his undertaking in committee, that if there is any suggestion of an undue paper burden remaining on small businesses, he will take the steps provided for in the bill to relieve that paper burden still further, and perhaps raise the threshold even higher. He has indicated from across the House that he is writing it in blood today. I am sure if we can get this minister to write such a commitment in his own blood-
I was touching wood!

The minister says he is touching wood. Perhaps that is something like what he has in his veins, I am not sure.
In short, I do not think there is any particular difficulty on our side of the House with the bill in its present form. I hope that in future years whoever has responsibility for this bill will always bear in mind that if it can be altered to relieve business still further from the necessity of having to file unnecessary paperwork, then at the earliest opportunity that will be done.

Mr. Speaker, we too are pleased that the government was willing when this bill was in committee to make a number of amendments to it and to make it a bill that is generally more acceptable.
Speaking on behalf of trade unions in this country, 1 can say that in general they do not like the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, but they would rather have it with the amendments proposed in Bill S-10 than as it stands at the present time.
Therefore, we are prepared to give third reading to this bill.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Acting Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-79, to amend the Veterans' Land Act and to amend the Veterans Benefits Act in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to introduce this bill today. It is a very complex bill in that it took about four or five years to get through it, legally and otherwise.
In proposing these amendments to the Veterans' Land Act, the government is acting to bring this legislation into accord with current social conventions. This legislation has been a valuable ally of veterans and their families for almost 40 years. Now, however, the act needs to reflect the changes that are taking place in our society.
Our amendments will ensure that the Veterans' Land Act no longer frustrates the aims of family law legislation in many provinces. In addition, these amendments will allow the veteran greater freedom in planning his estate. But as we move to amend the Veterans' Land Act, let us pause to review its benefits.
[ Translation]
Close to 144,000 veterans have been getting these benefits. In excess of $1.34 billion in public funds have helped to set up veterans on farms, on small homesteads or as commercial
July 8, 1981

fishermen and trappers. They have also been helped in continuing to be real Canadians and to be very active in today's society.
Even now, close to 38,000 veterans still live on properties which come under the Veterans Land Administration. Our country has gotten its fair reward. We also have gotten ours since so many gallant people have been able to settle on the land for which they had fought. Very few parts of this country have not benefited from the Veterans' Land Act, and this has resulted in a healthy growth for Canada.
Moreover, many of these small homesteads are now prosperous farms that are in a position to feed thousands of people overseas and to make a major contribution to our gross national product. However, in spite of its acknowledged success, the Act is now seen as inadequate by groups or individuals who are concerned about women's rights.

The spouses of veterans, the vast majority of whom are women, enjoy no legal interest in the land on which they live. And as more than 90 per cent of all outstanding VLA agreements represent the matrimonial home, it is little wonder that our present legislation has been termed unjust in this area.
However, any shortcomings in the act have developed accidentally. The first priority of those legislators back in 1942 was to protect the veteran. The earlier Soldier Settlement Act had met with mixed success. The legislators wanted to restrict individual failures to a minimum. They surrounded the veteran land holder with safeguards.
As a result, whenever a veteran went to apply for a conditional grant and a subsidized interest rate loan, he also received protection. In a typical situation, the director of Veterans Land Administration purchased a property for the veteran and held title to it until the debt was repaid. The veteran was designated as a tenant at will and on a direct legal basis was considered to have no recognized financial interest in the property during the period of the contract. This arrangement ensured that the veteran was immune to any action taken by would be creditors.
In the early days of the VLA, such agreement was most beneficial both to the veteran and to the Crown. Both received considerable benefits. In the case of the veteran, the land was protected against any lien which could have represented a very heavy responsibility for the veteran leaseholder. As for the Crown, it merely could regain possession of the property and hand it back to another eligible veteran if need be.
However, Mr. Speaker, the spouse, the wife in most cases, had no right to any of the benefits provided in this mutually profitable agreement. Let us think for a moment of the case where the young wife had helped her husband with the downpayment for the purchase of the family home. Let us think also
Veterans' Land Act
of the rather frequent case of the wife bringing along property which would make the couple's farm more productive. If the husband was a veteran and if the couple decided to avail themselves of the benefits available under the Veterans Land Act in order to expand or improve their property, the wife had to waive any property right she had even to whatever assets she had personally contributed. Such a situation is not good enough today in 1981, but in 1942, the legislators did not see any harm in it. Times have changed.

But as we well know, society has changed and veterans are not isolated from the joys and disappointments of marriage. There has been a dramatic increase in the number of cases before the courts for divorce, legal separation and property settlement. And along with the increase in marital breakdowns has come the valid charge that the Veterans' Land Act is not in concert with today's realities.
The reason is that with no dower, homestead of family rights in the veteran's property, the spouse is clearly at a disadvantage. Such a situation contradicts the purpose of the far-reaching changes that have been made in family law legislation in a number of provinces.
Such provincial legislation states, in effect, that irrespective of who holds title to the matrimonial home the statutory presumption is that on divorce or on marriage breakdown each spouse is entitled to a one-half interest in the matrimonial home.
Even in provinces where such legislation exists, the VLA property is virtually immune to the joint ownership principle. The wife can ask the court to declare that she has an interest in the property to be held in trust by the veteran, but this involves expensive legal action and many spouses are unaware of the legal intricacies. In addition, any interest she may receive will be of no benefit until the loan is repaid.
Away from the unhappiness of a family court, our present legislation can be a source of irritation for those many couples who still enjoy a happy marriage. By restricting the property agreement to the veteran alone, and by making him, in effect, a tenant on his own land, the legislation hampers estate planning.
[ Translation]
The Government has been trying for some time now to find an honourable and efficient way of solving this problem. We had to protect the vested interests of veterans in wartime while acknowledging the justified claim of the spouse who was not a veteran. More specifically, the properties involved are as much owned by the Crown as this Parliament. Mr. Speaker, I think that this amendment is the logical and acceptable solution under the circumstances.

Lirst, we are proposing to amend Section 37 of the act in order that the spouse has rights in the matrimonial home as provided by provincial legislation.

July 8, 1981
Veterans' Land Act
f Translation]
For equity's sake, Mr. Speaker, we also suggest a second amendment. It would allow the voluntary conversion of the sale contract to a mortgage when a 10-year conditional grant had been received. There is no change whatsoever in the interest rates provided for in the contract. Such a conversion to a conventional mortgage is acceptable to many veterans and their spouses anxious to hold the titles on their assets and funds as well as their ownership rights.

Before concluding, 1 would like to state that prior to introducing this legislation we consulted with the Royal Canadian Legion, the veterans' association and the commission on the status of women who reacted favourably to this bill. I am sure we can agree that this is a good bill and that it should be passed quickly.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to reply on behalf of Eler Majesty's loyal opposition with respect to Bill C-79. As a veteran I have a personal interest in veterans' legislation and it is with real interest and concern that I address this bill. It is a bill I think veterans will approve and it is one lawyers will also applaud. I shall return to this aspect later in my remarks.
Before I address the various provisions of this bill-and I say this for the interest of the Chair-I would like to make a few favourable and complimentary comments on the Veterans' Land Act, its implementation, application and administration. These comments should make it clear why the PC party supports the proposed legislation.
It is a sad fact of life that memory is imperfect. Few, if any, could reconstruct with accuracy what it was like to return to Canada following the Second World War, or, conversely, what it was like to welcome home the veterans of foreign wars. Major readjustments were necessary for both veterans and civilians.
Fortunately, Parliament had acted three years earlier to pass the Veterans' Land Act, a major rehabilitation program designed to assist veterans in their return to civilian life. Under this act a veteran could receive financial assistance to purchase land for the purpose of full or part-time farming or commercial fishing. The financial assistance received would be repayable in the same way a mortgage would, save that title to the property would be held by the director of the Veterans' Land Act until such time as the veteran had repaid the loan.
Subsequent amendments to this act extended its provisions to include veterans of the Korean war and to assist those veterans wishing to construct their own homes.
By making funds available to veterans to acquire land, the Veterans' Land Act enabled some 144,000 of our veterans to re-enter civilian society quickly and productively. Indeed, in 1980 there were still over 40,000 veterans covered under the act.
With the passage of time it became necessary for Parliament to commence the phasing-out of this program. As a
result, in March, 1977, loans under the act came to a halt, meaning that we have entered the final phase. Once all loans have been repaid and all titles to the various properties transferred, the Veterans' Land Act will for all intents and purposes have completed its job. This is expected to occur in the year 2007, 26 years from now.
Over the years since its enactment in 1942, the administration of the Veterans' Land Act has been excellent. The Auditor General's report spoke highly of the program and, to my knowledge, the Royal Canadian Legion has never had a serious complaint with the administration of the program. Hence, it is to the credit of the department that we can attribute the success of the Veterans' Land Act. All of which is not to say that updating amendments are not necessary, and it is to the legislation before us that I would now like to direct my comments.
Bill C-79 will be welcomed by many segments of our society. Lawyers will be happy to see the end of the cumbersome and long forms of agreement they were never able to explain to veterans. By virtue of the changes in this bill, veterans will be enabled to acquire title in their own right to the land which they occupy by way of deed. They will be able to show whatever debt or encumbrance is registered against those lands by way of charge or mortgage, just as any other person can do.
Spouses of veterans, most of whom are women, will welcome the bill, bringing as it does today's concept of spousal rights in property that she probably spent years in assisting to improve. This was a major recommendation of the Progressive Conservative Party and this minister's predecessor in office, the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon). Only in one area do I have a question, and that question relates to Clause 7 which repeals former Section 24 and substitutes a new Section 24. This section refers to the sale of lands held by the director under a contract with the veteran and where, as a result of that sale, there are moneys owing to the veteran, a surplus if you will, after the payment of debts and costs accruing to the veteran. That surplus is due and owing to the veteran.
The section goes on to provide that where the sale is made on a term basis, the director may make payment to the veteran, as the director determines payment to be warranted. I know what is intended here. It is that payment cannot be made to the veteran until payments under that term agreement are received by the director. However, it seems to me that the section could have been phrased differently to avoid what appears to be an absolute discretion in the director to pay over the surplus moneys dues and owing to the veteran, at a time when the director at his own discretion feels payment is warranted. The clause could even go on to say that the director should make payment to the veteran as payments are received by the director, and I trust that the minister will find time to take the opportunity to give the House some assurance on that particular point.
As I stated earlier, the Veteran's Land Act was a singularly good one, as has been its administration. The long-standing
July 8, 1981

complaint of the Conservative party, that the act did not address itself to the rights of the spouse, has now been answered and, as such, we are happy to lend our support to the bill.
It would be remiss of me, however, amid all the magnanimity, not to say that, with the spirit of co-operation which the government now sees from the Conservative party, we expect additional veterans' legislation to follow. Specifically, given the advancing age of our veterans, the phasing-in period of the provisions of Bill C-40 regarding widows whose husbands were in receipt of less than 48 per cent disability pensions should be shortened. The lengthy pension application delays are fast approaching the level of a national disgrace and we would expect the government to act quickly on this matter.
Further, the payment of prisoner of war compensation should be changed to add to, not subtract from, disability pensions veterans might be seeking. It is ridiculous to speak of prisoner of war compensation when in fact the resultant payment is not better or worse than a disabled veteran would ordinarily receive.
Finally, in these troubled financial times pension increases should be based on a meaningful index that will reflect current inflation rates, not the government's chimerical hopes. We hope the amendments presented will remedy some of those complaints. Bill C-79 is a good bill. It is one that follows the recommendations of this party and I look forward to the introduction of those further amendments in the very near future. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank the minister through you.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to indicate our full support for Bill C-79 which is now before us. If it is possible to be happier still, that is what I shall be in a day or two when we have before us Bill C-82. It will be a day to which I look forward.
My hon. friend, the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid), expressed a hope about Bill C-82. The only advantage I have over him is that it got first reading today and I have seen it. I notice he was asking for the phasing-in period to be shortened. It has been wiped out altogether. That is not related to this bill, Mr. Speaker, but it is pretty important news and that bill will get speedy passage in this House of Commons.
What is before us now is Bill C-79 which has to do with the Veterans' Land Act. Like the minister who spoke in introducing this bill, like the hon. member for St. Catharines who spoke in support of it, I too want to say this has been a very important piece of legislation, passed back in 1942, the year I was first elected to this House, though it was passed before I got here. It has been of great benefit to veterans and their families across the years.
We were pleased during a certain period in the life of this Parliament, 1972 to 1974, known as the minority period, that we were able to get an extension to the lifetime of the Veterans' Land Act. We wish we could have had it extended longer, but at least it did delay a bit the cutting off of the benefits under that act.
Veterans' Land Act
As the minister has pointed out, there are still 38,000 cases where the title is still in the hands of the director, and that makes the two changes which are presented to us today very important.
The first one makes this a great day for veterans. It also makes it another great day in a series of days that it seems to take to achieve equality between men and women. We make speeches about needing equality. We want it right away, but the facts of life are such that we have to take a step at a time. This is an important step, and I was glad to hear the minister say that not only had he been in consultation with the Legion and other veterans' organizations, but he had also been in consultation with women's groups as well.
One understands that 40 years ago the legislation provided for the land to be that of the veteran without any special rights for the spouse, especially if there was a breakdown in marriage or if the spouse was left a widow. But times have changed and it is good that we have caught up with one of those changes. In other words, the main thing this bill does is to establish for spouses of veterans, so far as the ownership of the land is concerned, the same rights in respect of VLA land that apply in the province to properties held under civil contract. This means that if there is a breakdown in marriage the spouse who has put a good deal into the development of the property can claim her share of it. It also means that if the veteran dies and leaves the spouse a widow, her rights to that property are continued.
The other main aspect of the legislation is to provide that for a veteran who is alone, or a veteran and a spouse, the ownership of the property, instead of continuing as though he or they were just tenants on land owned by the director, would have the conventional mortgage relationship, so that a veteran or the survivor could make a sale or use the value of the VLA holding in planning the estate, planning retirement or transferring it to somebody else, and so on.
All told, this is a good piece of legislation. Though the motion before us calls for the bill to be referred after second reading to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, I am sure I speak for all of us in the House when I say I would be quite happy to have it go into a Committee of the Whole in order to complete the full passage of this bill at this time.
I say again how important the Veterans' Land Act has been as a piece of veterans legislation. We are glad we are making these improvements to it. As the last speaker said, there are other matters still to be dealt with. We will deal with one of them when we get to Bill C-82, whether tomorrow or Friday. Then there are other questions, such as the speeding up of the handling of cases by the Canadian Pension Commission, and the fundamental issue of tying the rate of the 100 per cent war disability pension to the level of those five designated categories so that the increase of those pensions is automatic.
Those matters are not before us today, but the last thing I would want to do would be to give my friend the Acting Minister of Veterans Affairs the impression that the job is

July 8, 1981
Veterans' Land Act
done. He has done well to have these two matters before us now, second reading of this bill and first reading of Bill C-82 on the same day, but there are other things to do. I am sure he has the interests of veterans and their families at heart and, when we get these bills out of the way, we will be ready to move on.
As I say, we are quite prepared that this bill now be given second reading, that it be considered in Committee of the Whole and that it be given third reading this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, there is a little difficulty here since property rights are a provincial matter. There is nothing in the federal act which could defeat, for instance, a spouse's dower rights in a property occupied by a veteran and his spouse, although the property was in the name of the director. I am confirmed in that.
Subsection (2), appearing at line 28 says, and I quote:
Notwithstanding any other provision of this Act, an order made or a judgment rendered by a court of competent jurisdiction to recognize or enforce the rights, interest or estate of the spouse or a dependant of a veteran in land that is the subject of a contract of sale, mortgage or hypothec under this Act applies to and is binding on the land subject to the rights, interest or estate of the director in the land.
So therefore those dower rights and what have you are not wiped out. The director has an interest in them, just like a mortgage company has an interest in land which is ahead of dower rights, provided the spouse has signed her consent under dower legislation. In any event, with the greatest respect, I cannot see how any federal act dealing with land could affect property rights in any of the provinces. Therefore, such spouse interest that arises under a dower act, as in the province of Alberta, my own province, could not be defeated by any legislation in this House. However, there is, in my humble opinion, no such attempt here. The legislation here only confirms what is in existence.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the new provisions in this particular bill will be advantageous with respect to current cases and cases in the future, but our veterans are largely from the Second World War. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Would the hon. member repeat his question so that my official can understand exactly his meaning?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I would be glad to, Mr. Chairman. The provisions of this bill now make certain benefits available to spouses. These benefits have not been available to spouses since 1946 and will not be until this bill becomes law. Conse-
July 8, 1981

quently, there have been some very sad cases. Is there any provision in this bill which would make it possible to go back and rectify some of the things which have happened?

speechtext: Yes, it is out.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
That is rather sad because the bill comes in just about 30 years too late to help many people. I do not know whether the minister and his officials are aware that there may only be a handful, but there have been some cases which have been very unfortunate and sad.
We like to treat our veterans and their spouses in a way we can be proud of. Since almost 40 years have gone by since the end of the war-there are very few veterans left from the First World War-it seems to me that where there is definite evidence that something has been done which should be rectified, if that could be done it would certainly be appreciated by veterans all over Canada who do not have any particular interest in this bill at the moment.
In many cases civilization is recognized by the way we treat our senior citizens and our veterans, particularly our veterans, because they are a particular class in this country. All veterans offered their lives to the country and so they are in a particular group. Their wives and children have suffered in a particular way over the years because many veterans left part of their lives on the battlefields. I realize retroactivity is difficult, but I would greatly appreciate it if the minister could at least look at some of these cases to see if something can be done for the very sad cases that occurred because these provisions were not available.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, coming back to the question I raised before, I wonder if the minister has considered the situation of a mortgage, for instance, or any transfer from a veteran to the director on a financing transaction. If in the province of Alberta it did not contain a consent under the dower act, I am afraid the director would have been in very serious trouble. There is no way a federal law could unilaterally set aside that right of dower. That applies to anyone and everyone.
I may come back to that question because I do not think, in essence, there is very much difference now. If there had not been consent by the spouse under the dower act, or if the veteran was single at the time he sold or financed the property,
Veterans' Land Act
with the director, then possibly the law is now being changed somewhat, but not that much.
The other very interesting point, one that no one has yet raised, is in clause 9 at the top of page 7, the definition of "spouse". Perhaps the minister would like to indicate there whether this is recognizing the, shall we say, social consideration of the so-called common law spouse in that there is provision that if her interest is recognized under the laws of a province concerning land, then naturally such an interest is recognized under the Veterans' Land Act. I think that is a step forward, although I must say I have taken grave exception, and still do, to the changes in the Veterans Insurance Act and other veterans' benefits. A veteran living common law for, in one case, one year, in other cases for three years, can set aside all the rights of a legitimate spouse who has raised a family and lived with the veteran for many years. Then the veteran for one reason or another decides to cultivate greener fields and perhaps recycle himself with a younger woman, and thereby defeats all of the legitimate interests of his spouse. I was absolutely astounded that my good friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, did not raise an objection. I voted against it as I would right now if it were up to me because I think this is an absolute disgrace in our veterans legislation.
There are two areas of disgrace in our veterans legislation. One deals with the interests of the legitimate spouse of a veteran. Under the disability act, the Veterans Insurance Act and possibly one other act, a veteran living with a woman who is not his legal spouse gives her rights which extinguish the rights of the legal spouse. I think this is bad law, and I would hope some time to have the opportunity of discussing this with the minister so we can go back to what it was before, namely living together openly for seven years. I hope when we get to Bill C-82 that the minister, a former prisoner of war, will see the grave injustice done to POWs under the prisoners of war compensation act, more than 70 per cent of whom are pensioners and who find themselves disentitled either to a portion of their disability pension or of their compensation. The two are supposed to be separate, yet in the minds of the department they have been melded for these years. I hope we will have an opportunity to discuss that.
In this particular instance I think there has to be a consideration. There is no indication as to the time involved in this common law arrangement, or under what circumstances it would apply. speakeroldname: Mr. Raymond Savard (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I sponsor today Bill C-81, to amend the Official Residences Act. Since the act was implemented in its amended form in 1970, the Department of Public Works has been responsible for providing the services required for the official residences, and the National Capital Commission has been in charge of the maintenance and improvement of the grounds on which these residences are located. As parliamentary secretary, and speaking on behalf of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove), who is also responsible for the National Capital Commission, I believe that Bill C-81 contributes to reinforce the truly democratic parliamentary process which has long attested the strength of Canada.
Throughout the years, parliamentary proceedings have dragged on because of the increasingly complex issues brought before Parliament. In the past, sessions were shorter and recesses longer. However, our country's business now requires a total commitment on the part of parliamentarians.

Mr. Speaker, the bill which is before the House this afternoon deals with the establishment and operation of proposed embassies or consulates in Canada by persons not representing a sovereign state or not representing a government recognized by Canada.
The new legislation would make it an offence to engage in such conduct, enabling the courts to prohibit the representation of such premises as a diplomatic mission or a consular post. Actually, this bill seeks to resolve a sensitive problem which may occur at any given time and create for Canada some embarrassment on the international scene. Furthermore, such a situation would most likely create tension in Canada's bilateral relations with the country concerned.
I should point out that the Vienna conventions on diplomatic and consular relations annexed to the Diplomatic and Consular Privileges and Immunities Act are declaratory of customary international law and have the force of law in Canada. It is clear in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Regulations, Article 2:
the establishment of diplomatic relations between states and of permanent diplomatic missions takes place by mutual consent.
Article 4( 1) of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations provides that
"a consular post may be established in the territory of the receiving state only with that state's consent."
It would certainly be consistent with the spirit of Canada's obligations under the Vienna conventions to take the necessary measures to prevent the opening of such so-called embassies or consulates when they are opened without Canada's consent, and when they purport to represent a country or a government not recognized by Canada.
Let me point out, in conclusion, that the legislation is not directed against any particular group by name. It therefore should not affect the present representation of Baltic States in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-14, an act to amend the Diplomatic and Consular Privileges and Immunities Act, has the support of members of my party. We would like to see speedy passage accorded to it through all stages of legislation. The bill has emerged several times on the legislative docket in previous Parliaments, and, indeed, was introduced into the other place by the Clark government as Bill S-ll and given first reading on November 29, 1979.
The major thrust of the bill is to make it an offence to establish or to continue the operation of an embassy or consulate in Canada by persons not representing a sovereign state or a government recognized by Canada. From time to time, as we are aware, political groups and movements emerge which claim the right to full diplomatic recognition by other states and all the perquisites and prerogatives which accompany such an action.
It is proper that Canada state in legislative terms that no person or group of persons who do not represent a sovereign state shall have those privileges, so that any questions of doubt which linger in the minds of persons or organizations that do not enjoy legislative sovereign authority shall be laid to rest once and for all as far as this country is concerned.
As the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Duclos) has said, the Vienna Conventions on Diplomatic and Consular Relations set out the premises on which missions can be established, and Bill C-14 reiterates those understandings.
We would not want to see diplomatic or consular rights accorded to representatives of other than a sovereign state in this country, and in the same manner we would not tolerate that such recognition be given by other countries to groups or movements which might originate in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am rather surprised to be speaking again this afternoon. I thought we had a lot of business, and the House has indicated, by passing a number of bills that Parliament does live and that occasionally we do get through many pieces of legislation.
Last night I made a certain observation, and I am sorry that I have to make it again this afternoon in a different context. The fact that the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) has finally shown up does not mean I will terminate my remarks now, after all those points of order. I intend to conclude my remarks. This bill is an important piece of legislation, as I said last night. I say it again today and I have said it before. I have said it on a number of occasions, as have other members of our party and other members of Parliament and as has been indicated by many members of the government party. I know that ministers from time to time have obligations and appointments to keep and occasionally they find it impossible to be in the House. This afternoon we have seen examples of parliamentary secretaries coming to the
