House on what I would term not major bills, but bills that have received general consent in the House, technical bills on matters of lesser importance in terms of issues, but rarely do we see a situation when a major social or economic bill comes forward and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) refuses or neglects to be in the House of Commons during the course of the debate. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Irwin) is not even here to represent the minister. I thought it was bad enough last night that the parliamentary secretary led off this debate because there are important issues involved and there are important questions which arise by virtue of this legislation. The minister should be present to get the sense of the representations being made by members of Parliament who are dealing with this matter. I think it is incumbent on the minister himself to be present during the course of this debate.
I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice is now entering the House and I will retract my observations of him. But the minister was here today. His parliamentary secretary cannot say that the minister is not in Ottawa. The minister was present during question period. Maybe he is a little cowed or feeling somewhat hesitant about coming back to the House after the way he performed during question period. But the minister should be here for this legislation. I take particular exception to the fact that the minister is ignoring this legislation, and I reiterate that when we are talking about an important bill he should make up his mind whether or not he is interested in this portfolio. If he is not interested, then he should tender his resignation to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) so that we can have someone on the treasury benches who is interested in the legislation.
Last night when I was interrupted by the bell, I was addressing some of the provisions of the bill before us relating to the amendments to the Criminal Code, particularly Sections
246.1	and 246.2. I was pointing out some of the concerns I had with respect to the operation of those new provisions. I generally support the thrust that is being taken, but I think we have to be careful, in our consideration of this legislation, to make sure that the best possible legislation is produced by the House of Commons and that it is legislation which will have the proper effect in carrying out the intentions of Parliament. I was talking about my concern with respect to some of the definitions and the precision of the definitions within the bill itself.
At the conclusion of yesterday's proceedings I pointed out that the term "sexual assault" is not defined in this legislation. The bill simply says that everyone who commits a sexual assault is guilty of an indictable offence.
There are real questions as to just what sexual assault is. The elements of the offence are not laid out within the legislation. For example, if a person, in an effort to strike another in the stomach, misdirects that blow and it lands in the groin area, how is that defined? Is it sexual assault under the definition of the bill? I point out that the Law Reform Commission's recommendations contain a clearer statement of the requisite mental attitude in committing the crime of sexual
assault. I think that is important. After all, in the context of criminal law we are dealing with the intention of the accused in each instance. That is the general principle we have in criminal law under our system. The commission suggested that the code should read:
Everyone who, for a sexual purpose, directly or indirectly touches a person-
It goes on to say then that that person commits an offence. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that when we have an opportunity to look at this matter in committee, if that is possible during this session of Parliament, we will have to look carefully at the wording of Section 246.1 when studying this bill.
There is also considerable room for questioning the merits of the way in which the term "aggravated sexual assault" is defined in Section 246.2. This most serious offence comes into play only when a weapon is used during the assault or when serious bodily harm is caused. This formulation ignores entirely the issue of psychological harm as far as the complainant is concerned and it also ignores the conduct of the assailant, short of that which causes serious bodily harm. Let me deal with those two questions.
I think we should consider the inclusion of the notion of psychological harm under Section 246.2. Women are often advised not to resist a sexual attack so as not to suffer physical injury. That is not to say, however, that they may not be injured in a very real sense. An assailant who uses verbal threats or abuse can severely traumatize a victim and cause profound and lasting emotional damage. Statistics indicate that in 70 per cent of the cases that is the situation. It seems strange that an attacker who carries a knife but causes no physical injury would be liable to prosecution under Section 246.2, but an attacker who completely terrorizes a victim with verbal abuse and threats, and perhaps even forces a woman, through these threats, to commit particularly perverse or degrading acts would be liable only to punishment under Section 246.1.
These problems have to be looked at to make sure that we are not getting ourselves into the preposterous situation where the law is attempting to do one thing but has the consequence of reducing the kind of charge that may be placed against a person in a very serious set of circumstances. The specification of serious bodily harm in Section 246.2 must also be examined. This is a new and novel concept. The code presently uses the phrase "bodily harm" in Section 245. It does not contain any reference to serious bodily harm. This is a new term which takes us into uncharted waters. This is something which should be considered by the committee.
This bill changes the sentence for punishing persons who commit equivalent offences under the existing code. In some instances the penalties are higher under this bill and in some they are lower. For example, rape is now punishable by life imprisonment. Under the new system, sexual assault would carry a ten-year penalty. These are serious matters. I am sure that the members of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs will want to consider the extent and nature of
July 8, 1981

the penalties and sanctions placed in the code in respect of these offences.
I understand the rationale behind the remarks of the parliamentary secretary and indeed behind the material sent out by the Department of Justice. These are serious offences. We must look closely at them and be able to satisfy ourselves that the appropriate penalty is being placed with respect to each of the offences that are created under this bill and in the subsequent amendments to the act.
Another area of the bill I want to consider today deals with the way in which complainants are dealt with during trial proceedings. As 1 remarked yesterday, rape trials in particular often take on the appearance of being an inquisition into the private and personal life of the victim rather than an assessment of the case against the accused. This situation is most regrettable and no doubt it accounts in large measure for the fact that only one out of eight rape cases are reported.
Victims simply do not want to subject themselves to the trial process. That is understandable. It is a very traumatic experience for many women. They have to go through the process of a lengthy trial. They are placed on the stand. They find this a very trying time, as well as the preliminary investigation where questions are asked by the police and others in positions of authority.
On the other hand, we must not lose sight of the rights of the accused. Sometimes it is very easy to miss the balance that is required in these matters. In attempting to solve one set of problems, other problems are created with regard to the basic and fundamental rights that an accused has traditionally had in this country. A delicate balance must be struck between the right of the accused to have a full and fair defence and the necessity of complainants not to be subjected to degrading or unreasonable treatment.
This bill contains a number of features aimed, to a greater or lesser degree, at the question of protecting the complainant and eliminating unrealistic roadblocks in the path of the prosecution. The bill specifies that corroboration is not required to obtain a conviction for a sexual offence. This provision is found in proposed Section 246.2. There is a further stipulation that no corroboration warning is required. However, subsection (2) makes it clear that a judge can still comment on the credibility of the witness. There are some troublesome problems associated with this proposal. First, it is badly drafted. Some simple but important changes are required to make the section clearer. More important, it is uncertain how this section will affect Section 586 of the code as it now reads. Section 586 states:
No person shall be convicted of an offence upon the unsworn evidence of a child unless the evidence ... is corroborated in a material particular by evidence that implicates the accused.
This section particularizes in the criminal law context the general provision contained in Section 16(2) of the Canada Evidence Act.
The problem is this. Section 586 and the proposed Section
246.3	are not compatible. Since victims of sexual attacks are often children and since attacks often take place in situations
Criminal Code
where there is no corroborative evidence, the corroboration requirements in Section 586 is an onerous one. Since Section 586 is more particular than the general provision advanced in this bill, it may well be interpreted as overriding the amendment proposed in Bill C-53. This issue will have to be taken up and an explanation given. Possibly there should be an amendment by the officials of the department and, hopefully, by the minister, if he sees fit to attend the committee meetings.
The second feature of Bill C-53 that relates to improving the lot of the complainant and streamlining the law to some extent is contained in what would become the new Section 246.4. This section in the words of the minister's information paper "abolishes" the doctrine of recent complaint. The section itself uses the word "abrogate". We must look closely at subsection (3) of Section 246.4. It provides that in certain proceedings where consent is an issue and where by virtue of subsection (2) evidence of a complaint could still be heard, a judge "is not required" to give the jury any direction respecting the lack of a complaint. There is a real possibility that this subsection will resurrect the present state of affairs whereby the fact that no complaint was made immediately after the incident can lead to an inference of consent.
The third matter I want to deal with in this part of my remarks concerns questions posed at trial about the previous sexual conduct of the complainant. Under the common law a denial of sexual contact with others by the complainant precluded any further inquiry into what was considered a collateral issue. It was also open to an accused to ask questions as to the complainant's general reputation for chastity as a matter going to credibility and consent. The accused was entitled to bring evidence to contradict an accusation of lack of chastity.
In 1976 the government attempted to put limits on questions about the complainant's sexual relations with persons other than the accused. Section 142 of the code was introduced to achieve this end. It provided for notices of questions and an in camera assessment by a judge as to whether the questions should be asked in open court. However, the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in Forsythe v. The Queen (June 27, 1980) had the effect of making Section 142 much less effective than had been hoped. Under the terms of the Supreme Court's ruling, an accused can now force a complainant to answer questions in open court and can adduce evidence to contradict her answers.
This bill contains a section which is aimed at narrowing the scope of questions about a complainant's conduct with persons other than the accused. Section 246.5 would require written notice of questions and would require that a judge assess their merit at an in camera hearing at which the complainant would not be a compellable witness. Questions could only be asked in certain specified situations.
I think that these are welcome changes. They do, however, raise an issue which will need to be canvassed. It has been suggested that a complainant's sexual activities with persons other than the accused should be facts that are simply not admissible. The argument is that a person's activities with third parties are quite irrelevant to the question of consent with the accused. I am sure that this is a matter that will be

July 8, 1981
Criminal Code
convassed not only on the floor of the House, but also in the course of the committee hearings.
Another issue that has sparked a good deal of public debate in recent times concerns the defence of mistake of fact. In May, 1980, the Supreme Court of Canada ruled that the defence of mistake of fact was available to persons charged with rape. That is the Pappajohn case. The Pappajohn case held that an honest belief was sufficient and there was no additional requirement that it be reasonable. The decision prompted many people, women's groups in particular, to declare that Canada's rape laws had been eviscerated.
On the other side of the question, people argued that triers of fact are not so gullible as to believe pure fabrication and that the basic principles of criminal law as delineated in cases like Regina v. Beaver required that an honest belief must be sufficient.
[DOT] (noo)
This bill does not change the law and demand that a mistake of fact be reasonable. Rather, in Section 244(5), it provides that, where the defence is raised, the trial judge shall direct the jury when it determines the honesty of the belief to consider, inter alia, the presence or absence of reasonable grounds for that belief.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that we will have to submerge ourselves in the problems and controversies generated by the Pappajohn decision. I would suggest, however, that there are more than just two sides that can be taken. I think we may want to give some consideration to a third option which would involve a reverse-onus clause. Such a position would involve leaving the defence of an honest but unreasonable mistake open, but would force accused persons who want to avail themselves of such a defence to establish the existence of the mistake on a balance of probabilities. This is a middle-of-the-road position. Although it does not give accused persons the benefit of the doctrine whereby criminal offences must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt, it does leave the "mistake of fact" defence open, and at the same time it should answer most of the concerns of those who see the Pappajohn decision as a threat. The committee will hopefully consider this option when it grapples with the issue of mistake of fact, which was raised by members of the Senate in respect of this legislation.
As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, this bill deals with more than just sexual offences. I want to look now at those parts of the bill which deal with the abduction of children. We are all aware, I think, of the tremendous problems and heartbreak of many parents when a spouse abducts a child during the course of, or after, a custody dispute. Such actions are generally considered by the police to be matters for resolution in the civil courts. As a result, many people are simply left helpless. They lack either the resources or the legal recourse to recover their children by way of civil process.
The code does presently have a provision that covers abduction or harbouring of a child under 14. However, Section 250 is defective because it does not apply to persons "claiming in good faith" a right to possession of the child.
Bill C-53 proposes to deal with the problem of parents abducting children by introducing new Sections 250.1 and
250.2	to the Criminal Code. These provisions make the force of the criminal law available to persons faced with parental kidnapping. I welcome this attempt to combat a problem of growing seriousness in this country.
I should mention that one of my colleagues has taken a leading role in respect of encouraging this House to pass legislation, through many private member's bills, on this particular topic, and I refer to the hon. member for Surry-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen). Since the time he has been elected as a member of Parliament in 1974, he has continuously pressed the House of Commons through private member's bills to pass legislation which would afford some protection to parents in the case of parental kidnapping. I compliment the member because I am certain that it is because of the persistence he has demonstrated with regard to this particular change that the government has now seen fit to bring forward legislation in the course of these amendments which in effect try to deal with the problem.
I am not going to read Sections 250.1 and 250.2 into the record. However, I do want to point out one matter which should be looked into at the committee. I think we will want to re-word Section 250.1(1). It does not apply in cases where the parent with lawful possession of a child consents to the taking of the child from him or her. In many situations of kidnapping the parent in lawful possession does agree to the taking of the child by the other parent. Visits and outings are common. It is only when the other parent retains custody of the child that the problem arises.
My point is that the word "taking" as it is used in Section 250.1 is arguably not broad enough to cover the situation where a parent obtains permission to have the child for a period of time and then never returns that child.
I now want to speak about the provisions in the bill with regard to child pornography. So-called "kiddie porn" is a major concern in Canada. It is a problem that has been spreading and growing. The Criminal Code has no provisions aimed expressly at preventing the exploitation of children for pornographic purposes.
I am pleased to see that this bill makes an effort to hit directly at the problem. Happily, Mr. Speaker, the bill takes the right basic approach. It focuses on the aspect of exploitation and properly treats the children involved as victims.
This bill, C-53, proposes that a section 168.2 be added to the code. The section would make it an offence to induce, coerce or use a person under 16 years of age for the purpose of producing visual material containing what is referred to as "sexually explicit conduct". The bill would also create offences relating to the sale and distribution of material containing depictions of such conduct.
There is just one point I want to make about these proposals. As I indicated, these changes in the law are welcome indeed. There are, however, some problems 1 wish to point out. The section only relates to conduct of a sexual nature. I think
July 8, 1981

we must deal with the question of violence in this regard. A child can be portrayed as a participant in scenes of violence that are as obscene as those of a sexual nature. Sometimes 1 think we tend to become preoccupied with sexual matters in our society and concerned about that, and not in terms of criminal legislation having regard to the kind of programs now available generally through television and other forms of publication, theatre and movies. It often occurs to me, as I am sure it occurs to many other members, that the most repugnant kind of obscenity that can be observed in terms of television, theatre, movies and so on, is not necessarily that with a sexual connotation, strangely enough, but in terms of violence now being portrayed in our country in this way, and easily available and accessible to our children. This is something to which we may want to turn our attention to see whether there is something which can be done in this area in terms of amendments to the Criminal Code. We might address ourselves to what I consider to be an equally disturbing aspect affecting our society today.
The bill before us is, indeed, a very important one. I want to sit down soon in order that my colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo, can carry on in accordance with an agreement made in the House earlier and address his remarks to the House.
I simply want to reiterate the fact that the bill has been the product of good intentions. The fact is, as I have tried to point out on a number of instances, and occasionally in some detail, there are some very serious problems in terms of the draftsmanship and in terms of accomplishing the best legislation which has to be looked at by the committee. There are some very serious questions about some of the provisions of the bill which cause concern to members on both sides of the House. The parliamentary secretary pointed out yesterday that he has some concerns at this stage, and that the government has had some concerns that will cause the government to propose some amendments to this legislation.
I am very much concerned that what is happening here is somewhat of a charade. The government has introduced this bill in the dying moments of this part of the session, late at night, an afterthought after a number of less important bills have been dealt with and disposed of or debated, as the case may be. Under all the circumstances, I really wonder whether this will get the attention it should get in terms of the public media. It is important that there be public input into the provisions of this bill and a public understanding as to what is being attempted. 1 personally have tried to communicate with a wide range of interest groups across the country in my role as justice critic for the Official Opposition. 1 have tried to hear from them as to what their attitudes are with respect to this legislation. Many of the points I have made in my presentation today are the result of direct representations and observations made by people involved in this area either through counselling, involvement in child welfare or involvement in the administration of justice generally. In this latter respect I refer to lawyers and bar associations. 1 want to extend to them publicly my appreciation. I have received excellent co-opera-
Message from the Senate
tion from many people across the country who have taken the time either to come and see me and my colleagues in my party or to write to me about this legislation.
I think we will be faced again with the prospect of having this bill debated on the floor of the House of Commons, referred to a committee and stacked up with other legislation which is now before the committee or awaiting conclusion of consideration by the committee. The point is that the bill will not in the course of this session of Parliament receive the full attention of the committee. We will be faced again with a new Speech from the Throne and a new Parliament and with starting again the process of trying to get this bill brought forward so that we can have the legislation dealt with, improved and passed. I simply say to those who may be following this debate by watching it or reading Hansard that my concern is that we may have just started on the first leg of a journey. I am under no illusions that there will be a conclusion of the consideration of this bill. I am very disappointed in the way it has been handled and in the lack of priority. 1 am disappointed that the minister did not even think it important enough to appear in the House at any time that this matter has been discussed or to participate directly and listen to some of the suggestions made. I and other colleagues will be speaking further about the bill. It is a terribly important bill to which we want to give careful consideration.
1 simply say to the government that I am disappointed very much in the way in which this has been handled and in the ad hoc arrangements the government has made with respect to the introduction of the bill. I simply tell the minister that if he does not appear before this debate is over in the course of the committee deliberations-if we are able to have those-he does not know what trouble is, uranium cartel or no uranium cartel.

Criminal Code CRIMINAL CODE

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO SEXUAL OFFENCES AND THE PROTECTION OF YOUNG PERSONS

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill C-53, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to sexual offences and the protection of young persons and to amend certain other acts in relation thereto or in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO SEXUAL OFFENCES AND THE PROTECTION OF YOUNG PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak about Bill C-53, which is certainly one of the most important bills to come before this House. It is a bill for which the women of Canada have been waiting far too long.
Before getting into the substance of my remarks I would like to associate myself with the concern expressed by the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) about the absence from this House of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) during consideration of this important bill. There is no question that that is regrettable and is an indication, unfortunately, that the minister does not take seriously the fact that this is a bill of considerable substance to the women of Canada. It is such not just to the women of Canada but to all Canadians.
I would also say as a preliminary matter, speaking as the justice critic of the New Democratic Party, that we believe this bill should be dealt with quickly in the House and referred to the committee where it can receive the very careful study and consideration it needs. While we support the principles underlying Bill C-53, there is no question that there will have to be improvements made in the committee. Having said that, I should note that we have agreed that we should be prepared to see this bill go to committee after one speaker from our party-namely me-has spoken, and in view of the fact that the hon. member for Saskatoon West has recognized the importance of the bill, I certainly hope he will permit this bill to go to committee where it might be considered at an early date.
I note that the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs is presently involved in consideration of freedom of information legislation and also, as I understand it, it will be dealing with legislation respecting young offenders, but I hope we will see this bill go to the committee at an early date and that following the needed amendments to the bill we will see it passed into law.
As I said, Canadian women have been waiting for some time for changes to archaic laws with respect to sexual offences. Hon. members will know that there have been two bills in the past three or four years, Bill C-52 and Bill C-51, and in addition, in the fall of 1978 there was a very comprehensive report on the subject of sexual offences issued by the Law Reform Commission. That report made a number of important recommendations, some of which are reflected in the content of Bill C-53. Others, unfortunately, are not. I will note just a couple of matters which, unfortunately, are not dealt with in the bill. There is no reference whatsoever in this bill to the
important issue of sexual harassment. This has become increasingly prevalent in Canada in recent months and years. The Canadian Human Rights Commission in its most recent annual report urged the goverment to take action quickly to deal with concerns about sexual harassment and particularly sexual harassment on the job. Unfortunately, the federal government has remained silent and has not responded to these concerns about sexual harassment in the workplace. There has been some indication that perhaps there may be changes to the Canada Labour Code, but there is no question that until legislative steps are taken, Canadian women will be subjected to sexual harassment. There must be an end to this practice very quickly.
I also note that there is no reference in this bill to Section 179(1) or Section 193 of the Criminal Code. These are sections of the code dealing with laws respecting what are known as common bawdy houses. I urge that in the context of our consideration of this bill, a bill which should deal comprehensively with sexual offences and matters relating to sexual offences, we review these provisions of the Criminal Code. Unfortunately there appears to have been a sweeping abuse of this law recently in the city of Toronto, in the city of Edmonton and elsewhere. When we review these provisions of the Criminal Code with respect to common bawdy houses, we should examine very carefully the definition of a common bawdy house and particularly whether the concept of an act of indecency-whatever that may be; it may very well be an act which is entirely legal in private-should continue to be included in the definition of a common bawdy house.
Finally, a matter which has been touched on only peripherally in the context of Bill C-53 is the matter of prostitution. This bill purports to attempt to equalize provisions of the Criminal Code and bring sexual equality to bear in the Criminal Code with respect to sexual offences. However, there is still a glaring inequity in the area of prostitution. While on the one hand a woman who is deemed to be pressing and persistent in attempting to seek a sexual liaison can be charged, a man, the prospective John as he is called, is immune from prosecution. So a man who harasses persistently and pressingly a woman going about her business, asks her if she wants to have a good time or solicits her for the purposes of sexual relations, is not covered by the provisions of the Criminal Code relating to prostitution. Surely that kind of double standard must be addressed in a bill purporting to bring equality to this area of the law.
I note there is a single reference to prostitution in the legislation which would clarify that the prostitute can be either a man or a woman. That is as it should be if there is to be equality in the law. At the same time we must recognize that the behaviour of a man who pressingly and persistently bothers a woman for the purposes of prostitution should be covered.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, the bill attempts to overhaul a number of areas of the Criminal Code, not just with respect to sexual offences. The first major provision of the bill is with respect to the sexual exploitation of young people and child
July 8, 1981

pornography. There are changes with respect to the gross indecency provision and others of a similar nature. There are changes relating to child abduction by a parent, indeed by another person. Of course we all know the great anguish that can be caused in circumstances such as this. There are changes with respect to evidentiary provisions in trials of sexual offences. Finally, and most important, there are changes with respect to rape laws, namely, a redefinition of the offences of rape and indecent assault. I say without hesitation that we welcome the changes to redefine rape as a crime of violence and aggression, not one of lust or passion. It is a violent crime, and to the extent this law recognizes that, the changes are welcome.
I also note a very significant change from earlier bills submitted by the Liberal government, a change in response to representations from many groups and individuals across Canada. That is the removal of the so-called spousal immunity, the doctrine that says a wife cannot be raped. In this day and age we must recognize that marriage should not mean forced sexual submission and to the extent that this bill removes spousal immunity from the law, we welcome the principle.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, also deals with certain archaic and, in many ways, sexist provisions of our rape laws. It gets rid of the outdated notion that rape can only take place if the penis penetrates the vagina and that a man can only rape a woman. It recognizes that as a sexist provision and that there can be a variety of forms of sexual assault.
Now I would like to return to some of the areas I dealt with in passing earlier. Naturally I will be elaborating in detail on some of the important aspects of the bill which require amendment if it is to reflect truly the views and concerns of all Canadians, not just of women. All members of the House will welcome the general thrust of the provisions concerning the sexual exploitation of young people. We recognize it is necessary to eliminate the sexist nature of the present law. There are many archaic notions in the Criminal Code with respect to sexual offences against young people, such concepts as the notion of a previously chaste character and others which discriminate on the basis of sex. However, there are still a number of problems with respect to the government's proposals in this area. The key concept is that of sexual misconduct. What is meant by that? Nowhere in the bill do we find any definition of sexual misconduct, whatever that may be. The Law Reform Commission suggested, for example, that the that concept of sexual contact should be invoked. By that they meant we would be referring to any touching of the sexual organs of another, or the touching of another with one's sexual organs that is not accidental. At least there we have some specific definition.
Of course, there may be problems with that as well. One can question, for example, whether we might wish to prohibit certain other conduct that does not involve specific contact of sexual organs, such as what has been known as french kissing, and other forms of sexual contact. In any event, there is no definition of this central concept of sexual misconduct. We will
Criminal Code
be seeking further clarification of it in committee. Similarly, Mr. Speaker, clause 167(2)(d), the reference to young people between the ages of 14 and 16 being, and I use the words of the clause, states:
-less responsible than the complainant for the sexual misconduct that took place.
What does this concept mean? This is a new concept in our law and one which may unfortunately involve in many cases, in effect, the placing of the young person on trial, questioning whether or not a 14 or 15-year old was more responsible for the sexual contact, whatever it may have been, than the older person.
There must be clarity in the law. This would appear to bring into force the old concept of "more to blame" an archaic concept which should be repealed in this day and age. No one questions that there must be tough and effective protection from sexual exploitation of young people. In this regard we welcome the establishment of a study committee on sexual abuse of children to be chaired, I believe, by Dr. Robin Badgley. However, the time-frame of two years for this particular study is far too long. Sexual abuse of children is rampant and widespread in Canadian society and must be put to an end quickly.
In this connection I would certainly hope, Mr. Speaker, that this important study, which hopefully will not take the full two years, will not be cut short the way the study of Corinne Robertshaw was cut short. In a disgraceful act, the hard preliminary work of a group of dedicated experts was brought to an end and Corinne Robertshaw was told to turn over to the government the raw material she had before she had written her final comprehensive report. This kind of contempt of a committee studying the important issue of child abuse must be recognized as such by members of this House. I strongly urge all members to encourage the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) to permit Corinne Robertshaw to continue her study.
I also note, Mr. Speaker, that the bill does not accept the recommendation made by the Law Reform Commission in 1978, a recommendation endorsed by the National Association of Women and the Law, and a number of other groups, that sexual intercourse with an adult blood relative should not be a criminal offence in this day and age. Without taking a firm position on that question, we will certainly want to hear witnesses as to whether or not it is appropriate that within the Criminal Code we define that kind of consensual adult behaviour in private as being of a criminal nature.
I mentioned the provisions of the bill related to the serious problem-and there is no question it is a serious problem-of child pornography in Canada. All members share the revulsion at the exploitation of children for the purposes of the production of pornography. I would note that in 1978 the unanimous report of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs recommended toughening the sanctions in this particular area. Without endorsing this time all of those recommendations, 1 would certainly say this is an area we will want to examine further in the committee to ensure that the provisions are

July 8, 1981
Criminal Code
drafted in a way which would effectively meet the very real concerns about this "kiddy porn", as it is known, which is, unfortunately, all too prevalent in Canadian society.
Another area which is touched upon in the bill, although not referred to by either the speaker on behalf of the government or of the Conservative party, is sections of the bill with respect to gross indecency. As the House will know, these provisions are very vague and in many ways archaic. 1 would point out that gross indecency has been judicially interpreted as covering conduct which "violates the general instinctive sense of Canadians as to what is decent and clean as distinct from what is indecent and dirty." Those words are from the leading decision on the subject of gross indecency.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, that definition is very broad and has been abused in a fashion which really constitutes discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. I would urge that these provisions be repealed, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) has urged in this House through a recent bill, that this particular provision be recognized as archaic, and that the behaviour which is attempted to be dealt with in this provision should, indeed, be covered by other sections of the proposed sexual offences legislation.
In this day and age it is most improper that there should be any laws which discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation. I would have hoped that a government, which talked in terms of a charter of rights for all Canadians, would recognize that provisions of the Criminal Code which discriminate on that basis, as does the provision with respect to gross indecency as it is applied in Canada, must be repealed. As I have said before, this is a provision which is archaic and discriminatory. Young people are adequately protected by other provisions in the sexual offences bill. I would urge the government to consider seriously repealing Section 158 of the Criminal Code.
I would like to say that the child abduction section which is included in the bill is a step in the right direction. Many of us are aware of the very serious problems which have been caused, and the great anguish which results, when children are abducted from the lawful custodial parent. They may be taken from province to province or, indeed, out of the country. Naturally, we will want to examine carefully whether the proposed penalties which are contained in this section are not excessive and whether the appropriate response in this area is, indeed, lengthy jail terms or whether, in recognizing that we must combat, and combat effectively, this serious problem of illegal child abduction there are other alternatives and other methods. I look forward to hearing from witnesses from a number of different organizations on this important question.
There are a number of evidenciary changes which for the most part we welcome, such as the overruling of the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in the Forsythe case, which in many ways reverted back to the pre-1976 period and put a woman on trial, treated the complainant, as it were, as essentially being a compellable witness. But the bill does not go far enough. The bill still states that the previous sexual history of
that woman with a person other than the accused should be admissible in evidence. 1 say very clearly that the evidence of a previous sexual history of a woman with a person other than the accused should not be admissible in a court of law when dealing with these sexual offences. Quite simply the issue is: was that woman assaulted on that particular occasion? Her history of sexual involvement with other men on other occasions must not be considered as relevant. Unfortunately, it has been the case on too many occasions that juries, and in some cases trial judges, I suspect, have failed to distinguish between the alleged purpose of such questions, which is allegedly to go to the issue of credibility. There is the general suggestion that somehow because a woman has had other sexual involvement, it was not as likely that she was sexually assaulted on that particular occasion.
Some months ago I raised in the House the case of a woman who was raped here in the Ottawa area. The man who was charged was ultimately convicted of that rape and was given a very light sentence. Mr. Justice Pennell stated that the woman who was raped was a "woman of the world", as he put it, and because she was a woman of the world that fact should be reflected in the sentence. That kind of judicial idiocy must be put to an end.
The doctrine of recent complaint, which is repealed by this bill, should have been repealed a long time ago. We welcome that repeal provision.
Clause 31 of the bill would make spouses competent and compellable witnesses in cases of violence against children. As I said earlier, we recognize the serious problem of the abuse of children. We welcome this change to the evidenciary provisions of the Canada Evidence Act. I hope this provision will cut down on the incidence of child abuse.
There is one final change in the trial procedures which allegedly deals with the Pappajohn decision, a decision handed down by the Supreme Court of Canada in June of 1980. This decision caused a serious setback to all Canadian women. I would briefly like to explain the effect of that decision. What the Pappajohn precedent made very clear was that if a man came into court and claimed that he honestly believed that a woman was consenting to an unwanted sexual assault, even if there were no reasonable grounds for that belief, he must be acquitted. In this decision, the Supreme Court of Canada followed the Morgan decision of the English House of Lords.
I would like to give one example of the devastating effect of the Pappajohn precedent in Canadian law. Shortly after the Morgan decision there was a decision known as Regina vs. Coggin in which a man, Mr. Leek, brought home a friend named Coggin. Both Leek and Coggin had been drinking. Leek's wife was at home and he told her that Coggin wanted to have sexual intercourse with her and that he, Leek, would also have sexual intercourse with her. The husband had sexual intercourse with his wife, after having beaten her, and then he turned her over, as it were, to his friend Coggin who had sexual intercourse with her. The whole time this was going on, Mrs. Leek was sobbing and she tried to turn away from Coggin. Coggin gave evidence at trial that he thought Mrs.
July 8, 1981

Leek had consented because her husband had said she would really enjoy the intercourse. This was the only basis for his belief that she was consenting. He was also drunk at the time.
Mr. Coggin walked out of the courtroom a free man on the basis of his belief, even though it was perverse and without any reasonable grounds, that Mrs. Leek was consenting to this act of violence, even though she put up resistance and cried. He was acquitted. This is the effect the Pappajohn decision will have on Canadian women.
Canadian women have clearly stated that no must mean no when dealing with rape law in Canada. I wish to give credit to the North Shore Women's Centre which has worked together with me to launch a national petition campaign to overturn this very dangerous and regressive precedent. Men and women, women's groups and other organizations, including the Canadian Association for the Status of Women, have signed this petition. Each day more people come into my office to sign it. At last count, there were over 20,000 signatures on the petition which demands that the government take action to reverse the Pappajohn decision.
What kind of impact will this bill have on the precedent? Unfortunately, it in no way changes the Pappajohn decision. I can assure Your Honour that we will be fighting, and fighting hard, on behalf of Canadian women and on behalf of the many organizations and individuals which have urged the government to reverse this precedent to ensure that in committee this kind of change is made and that this regressive Pappajohn precedent is, in fact, overruled.
The final area which is covered by this bill, and which is, in many respects the most important area of the bill, is clause 18. Clause 18 would redefine the crimes of rape and indecent assault as sexual assault and aggravated sexual assault. It would also eliminate spousal immunity, as I indicated earlier, and it would put an end to the sexist nature of this crime. I need give only one example. As it now stands, an indecent assault on a women is punishable by a five-year maximum sentence. An indecent assault on a man is punishable by a ten-year maximum sentence. It is that kind of inequality in our law to which we welcome changes, and this bill does, in fact, move in that direction. So there be no doubt, 1 immediately say that we welcome the changes with respect to the elimination of spousal immunity.
We recognize the important advance in redefining rape as a crime of violence and as a crime of aggression, and not as a crime of passion or a sexual crime. We welcome an end to the sexist nature of many parts of the Criminal Code. It has been said by a number of commentators that as often as every six minutes somewhere in Canada a woman is sexually assaulted. That works out to one out of every five Canadian women who will be assaulted against her will. I am now quoting that figure from an excellent series of articles by a Toronto journalist, Michele Landsberg. That figure does not even include the figure of rape, a crime which is inflicted on one out of every 17 women.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO SEXUAL OFFENCES AND THE PROTECTION OF YOUNG PERSONS
speechtext: Which series is that?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO SEXUAL OFFENCES AND THE PROTECTION OF YOUNG PERSONS
speechtext:
This was a four-part series written by Michele Landsberg appearing in the Toronto Star in May of this year.
It is also estimated that some 94 per cent of rapists go right on raping and, in fact, are not reported. I would like to give again one example from Toronto about the conviction of rapes in the rape area. In 1979, in Toronto, there were 207 alleged rapes which were reported. Of course, many more rapes occur than are reported. Of those 207 reported rapes, 87 men were charged. Of those 87 men who were charged, only 16 were brought to trial. Of those 16 who were brought to trial, only 12 were convicted of rape or, in some cases, of a lesser charge. Ultimately, out of 207 reported rapes-and, in fact, there is a far larger number of rapes-only 12 convictions were recorded.
To the extent that this bill attempts to encourage women to report rape, and to the extent that it will facilitate the conviction of those persons who are guilty of sexual assaults, we welcome these provisions. However, I urge the government to reconsider seriously the present classification of sexual assaults which is proposed in this bill, namely, only two broad categories: the category of sexual assault, with a maximum of ten years; and the category of aggravated sexual assault with a maximum life sentence.
I would point out that the category of sexual assault includes everything from unwanted grabbing and fondling which, indeed, must be considered to be a criminal offence, to what we now know as rape. Within that one broad, sweeping category there is far too much behaviour which 1 would urge should be broken down into at least three, and preferably four categories. The Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women recommended in 1978, and recently repeated the recommendation, that there should be four categories. While these may not be the final categories which are recommended certainly for the record, I would like to put them forward. The council proposes there be a category of sexual assault which would be an electable offence punishable on summary conviction or by indictment; sexual assault while armed with a weapon; sexual assault causing bodily harm; and finally, sexual assault with intent to maim or endanger life which would have a maximum sentence of life imprisonment.
However, in any event, many groups, and many women's groups in particular, have urged the government to change this section of the bill to broaden the category, and not to have only one sweeping category of sexual assault and another sweeping category of aggravated sexual assault.
I would also note that a concern has been expressed, one with which I associate myself, that in amending the Criminal Code in the area of sexual offences, we should not remove the all important right to trial by jury, wherever that right is presently afforded the accused. I would also point out that the bill, as it is now worded, would eliminate the offence of wounding and would rewrite the assault provisions of the Criminal Code. A number of concerns have been expressed to

July 8, 1981
Criminal Code
me with respect to the elimination of that particular offence, and we will want to hear carefully from witnesses, such as the Canadian Bar Association, and other witnesses, as to whether this is a wise course to take.
1 know that there has been some suggestion by some commentators that it is a mistake to change the name of the offence from rape to sexual assault or, indeed, to simple assault. Naturally we want to hear further evidence on this issue in committee, but on balance, though I certainly have an open mind on it, I am persuaded at this point that we should maintain the suggestion that we redefine the offence of rape as a crime of assault, and that in doing so, we call it that and recognize it as an assault.
Therefore, we welcome those changes to the provisions of the Criminal Code with respect to rape and the redefinition of rape. While those changes are important, there are at least a couple of other areas on which I would urge the government to take action, and it does not have to wait for the passage of this bill to do so. The first is with respect to increased education in the area of sexual offences and response to sexual offences on the part of the police and other individuals.
I would urge, as the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women has urged, that specific educational programs be developed for persons involved in the prevention of crimes of a sexual nature, and that there be assistance both to the victims of these crimes and also assistance to encourage people who are involved in them to undertake research to find out what it is that leads people to commit these crimes.
In addition, I would urge that the government consider funding programs which would assist persons who are specifically trained to deal with and provide information to victims of sexual offences, that there be such persons in all police departments, for example, and also that specific education be provided. There is a great mystique around this area, but there should be specific education for other professionals such as doctors and lawyers, to ensure that they are qualified to provide legal, physical and psychological assistance and information needed by victims of sexual assault and, as well, by offenders.
I would urge that there be far greater funding for rape relief centres in Canada. These centres often operate on a shoestring budget, and they do perform a very valuable service in assisting the victims of sexual assaults. I would note that in my own province, for example, the province of British Columbia, there are very few halfway houses which presently assist women in these circumstances, and they cannot even begin to accommodate the demand in this area. Therefore, I would urge the government substantially to increase its funding, on a cost shared basis where necessary, of rape relief centres.
Finally, I would suggest that the government seriously examine a precedent in the United States. In 1976, the U.S. federal government established a national centre for the prevention and control of rape. As we know, rape is the fastest growing violent crime in Canada and in the United States. In view of this, I would urge the government to consider seriously the possibility of establishing such a national centre, a federal
centre, for the prevention and control of rape. The American centre supports research into the causes of rape. It examines laws dealing with rape, laws dealing with the treatment of victims, and the effectiveness of existing programs to prevent and control rape. It involves itself in research and demonstration projects. It assists, through research and demonstration grants, local communities and mental health centres. Finally, it is involved in the dissemination of information with respect to the area of rape.
This is a serious offence. As I say, we welcome the changes in this law to the extent that they will reduce the incidence of sexual assaults of all nature in Canadian society. I would conclude by saying that we strongly support the principles underlying this bill. As I have indicated during the course of my remarks this afternoon, we seek a strengthening of a number of key positions. I mentioned the Pappajohn decision and the repeal of the sections with respect to gross indecency and an end to discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in all sections of the Criminal Code. I mentioned the strengthening of the provisions on sexual exploitation of young persons and, of course, there are a number of other areas on which we will hear from witnesses at committee.
We want this bill to go through and be improved in committee before the end of this session. The women of Canada have waited far too long for justice and for equity and for an end to sexist race laws.
I challenge the government to take seriously its commitment made in the Speech from the Throne to reducing the incidence of violence against women. In the event that we are not able to get this bill through before the end of this session, and that would be unfortunate, I urge the government to bring back before the House, as a top priority, another, stronger bill containing the same principles, at the earliest possible time in the new session.
This party is prepared to see the bill go to committee now. We have agreed to having one speaker on behalf of this party; we have heard one speaker from the Conservative party and one from the government side. I hope that all parties will recognize the urgency of overhauling the archaic laws of Canada with respect to sexual offences and would be prepared to see this bill go to committee now.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO SEXUAL OFFENCES AND THE PROTECTION OF YOUNG PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the debate and I want to commend hon. members for the high quality of their contribution on a matter of some considerable importance, not just to Canadian women but as well to the evolution of criminal law in Canada.
1 do not want the parliamentary secretary to take any offence at my next remarks because I know the position of parliamentary secretaries. They have to do what their ministers tell them or else they do not get reappointed. There are a number of hopefuls sitting on the back benches who would be quite happy to take their places. In fact, they are waiting for
July 8, 1981

the opportunity to advance if a parliamentary secretary does not do what his minister tells him.
1 think it is rather important that on a matter which is so significant, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) should present the bill, and that the Minister of Justice be present during the course of the debate. I want to commend ministers who have sat through long debates doing their duty and I want to contrast for members of the House on all sides, what has occurred in the passage of this bill.
In the first place, it was introduced by a parliamentary secretary reading from notes that were likely prepared in the Department of Justice. They may or may not have been prepared for the minister. The Minister of Justice was in the House during Question Period yesterday. His bill was introduced last night but he was not in the House then. He was present during Question Period today and answered questions on the uranium cartel matter which, quite rightly, seems to be engaging the attention of the House. However, rather than remaining to deal with this bill, the Minister of Justice disappeared. I do not know if he has involved himself in the investigations with respect to the uranium cartel, but he does this House, the women of Canada and his own portfolio a great disservice.
I believe I heard a knock from the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, Mr. Speaker.
